generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, research ethics is part of how good work is defined, not a hurdle cleared before the work starts. The school shares one focus, sport, physical activity, performance and health, but its subjects raise different ethical issues. A sport scientist draws blood and pushes participants to exhaustion, a coaching student films training, a management student surveys club members. Each must respect participants, secure informed consent, minimise harm, and report methods and findings honestly. The six ESRC principles underpin all of this, so an ethics application read as a design discipline rather than paperwork makes the research itself sounder.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students prepare the same VO2 max testing study on recreational runners for ethical approval.

Tom treats the ethics application as a form to clear. The consent wording says nothing about how performance data and health screening results will be stored, participation is described as expected of the sports-science cohort, and his role as the runners' strength coach goes unmentioned. The study may still gain approval, but it sits uneasily against the principles of informed participation, transparency and declared interest.

Amara reads her maximal-exertion protocol against each principle in turn. Participation is made genuinely voluntary and informed, the risks of exhaustive testing are spelled out, storage and responsibility are stated, and her coaching link to the runners is declared openly. Nothing about the study is hidden, so the application documents a design that is sound rather than merely permitted.

Both students will submit a form. Only Amara used the principles to improve the research itself, which is what treating ethics as integrity rather than paperwork means.
generatedProse.summary: Research ethics in the School of Sport is the substance behind the ethics form, not the form itself. You can now justify ethical conduct as an expression of academic integrity, evaluate a sport study against the six ESRC principles, and anticipate the issues an ethics application in sport must address. The next lesson turns to the duties you take on once you start collecting data from participants.

check.body: A sport and exercise science study plans to recruit participants by telling them their seminar tutor expects them to take part in a fitness-testing session. Which ESRC principle does this most clearly breach?

items.text: That participation should, wherever possible, be voluntary and appropriately informed.
That research should maximise benefit and minimise harm.
That lines of responsibility should be clearly defined.
That the independence of research should be maintained.

feedback.correct: That's right. Telling students a tutor expects participation makes it no longer freely voluntary.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Which principle is about the freedom to take part?
feedback.incorrectFinal: Recruiting through a tutor's expectation breaches voluntary, informed participation; the other principles are about outcomes, accountability and independence.
